name: User Simulation for Multi-Turn Agents
question: Does the agent still work when the user talks back?
summary: A single-turn test gives the agent everything at once. Real users reveal details slowly, change their mind, write in Hinglish, get impatient and make mistakes. User simulation has an LLM play the user from a scenario card: a persona, a goal, details it knows but reveals only when asked, and rules for when to stop. The simulated user and the agent talk for many turns, and the conversation is scored on the end state (was the refund raised, with the right amount) plus a rubric. Because both sides are stochastic, each scenario runs k times and reliability is reported as pass^k, the chance that all k runs succeed. Building the scenario set is covered by Eval Datasets; this technique is the multi-turn harness.
useCases: Customer support and booking agents that gather details over several turns
Checking behaviour with difficult personas before real users meet them
Regression tests for multi-turn policies such as refunds and KYC

items.detail: persona, goal, hidden details, stop rule and the expected end state
reveal details only when asked, stay in character, never solve the task for the agent
compare database or tool state with the expected one, not the transcript wording
probability all k runs of a scenario succeed; falls fast when agents are inconsistent
language, patience, expertise, mistakes; weighted like the real user base
the LLM user breaking character or leaking hidden details; audit a sample

steps: Write scenario cards from real conversations, with hidden details and expected end state
Prompt a simulator model to play the user, with rules against leaking or solving
Run each scenario k times and check end states in the backend
Report pass^1 and pass^k by persona, and read failed transcripts
pitfalls: Scripted user turns that never react to the agent, so every test passes
A simulator that reveals every detail in its first message, making the task easy
Only polite English personas when real users write in Hinglish and in a hurry
remember: An LLM plays the user; check the end state; repeat and report pass^k.
caption: Illustrative: Paisa Setu, a fictional UPI app, tests its refund agent on 200 simulated conversations.

code.text: CARD = dict(persona="impatient, writes Hinglish, not tech-savvy",
goal="refund for a failed ₹2,450 UPI payment",
SIM_RULES = """You are the customer. Stay in character. Reveal hidden details
only when the agent asks for them. Never solve the task yourself.
Say DONE when your goal is met or you give up."""
return backend.state_matches(card["expected"])     # check the end state
results = [[run(c, agent, sim) for _ in range(k)] for c in cards]
pass1 = sum(sum(r) for r in results) / (k * len(results))
passk = sum(all(r) for r in results) / len(results)

steps.title: Write a scenario card
steps.text: Paisa Setu, a fictional UPI app, writes cards from real chats: a persona, a goal, hidden details such as the UTR number, and the expected end state in the backend.

steps.title: Give the simulator rules
steps.text: The simulated user must stay in character, reveal details only when asked and never solve the task. Without these rules it pastes everything in the first message and the test is too easy.

steps.title: Let them talk
steps.text: The simulator and the agent exchange turns until the simulator says DONE or 12 turns pass. The agent has to ask for the UTR number, confirm the amount and raise the ticket.

steps.title: Check the end state
steps.text: Success is a refund ticket for ₹2,450 in the backend, not polite wording in the transcript.

steps.title: Repeat each scenario
steps.text: Each of 200 scenarios runs 4 times. pass^1 is the average success; pass^4 counts scenarios where all 4 runs succeed.

steps.title: Read the numbers
steps.text: With a realistic mix of personas, pass^1 is 71% (scripted tests said 95%) and pass^4 is only 25%: the agent is right most of the time but not reliably.

pros: Tests the multi-turn behaviour real users trigger
Cheap to run hundreds of conversations before launch
Personas expose failures with language, patience and mistakes
pass^k shows reliability, not just average success
cons: The simulator can break character or leak details
Scenario cards take effort to write well
Simulated users are still not real users
avoidWhen: Single-turn tools where one request carries everything
As the only evidence: also sample real conversations after launch

practice.scenario: Paisa Setu, a fictional UPI app, has a refund agent that passed 95% of its scripted tests yet struggled with real customers. It writes 200 scenario cards from real chats, each with a persona, a goal, hidden details such as the UTR number and the expected backend end state. An LLM plays each user, some in Hinglish and in a hurry, and every scenario runs 4 times. pass^1 is 71%, matching what real users see, pass^4 is 25%, and 18 of 20 known failure types surface before release.

industries.use: Refund and dispute agents that must collect UTRs, amounts and dates
Rebooking agents where users change their minds mid-conversation
Plan-change agents talking to users who are unsure what they want

practice.analogy: A mock customer at a training desk who has a secret receipt in their pocket and hands it over only if the trainee asks for it.

library.name: anthropic
library.what: Any chat model API can play the user; this example uses the Anthropic SDK for both the simulated user and a stub agent.

practice.note: The model name is an example; use one available on your account. my_agent.respond and backend.refund_raised stand for your own agent and backend check.

samples.code:
import anthropic
from my_agent import respond, backend        # your agent and backend check

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
CARD = ("You are a Paisa Setu customer. Persona: impatient, writes Hinglish. "
        "Goal: refund for a failed Rs 2,450 UPI payment. Hidden: UTR 417803921556; "
        "give it only if asked. Never solve the task yourself. Say DONE when finished.")

def sim_turn(history):
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5", max_tokens=200, system=CARD,
                               messages=history)
    return r.content[0].text

history = [{"role": "user", "content": "Start the chat."}]
user_msg = sim_turn(history)
for _ in range(12):
    agent_msg = respond(user_msg)
    history += [{"role": "assistant", "content": user_msg}, {"role": "user", "content": agent_msg}]
    user_msg = sim_turn(history)
    if "DONE" in user_msg:
        break
print("passed:", backend.refund_raised(amount=2450))

numericDrill.question: An agent succeeds on a scenario 71% of the time, independently per run. What is pass^4, the chance that all 4 runs succeed, as a percentage?

interview.question: Why simulate users with an LLM instead of scripting turns?
interview.answer: Scripted turns do not react to what the agent says, so an agent that forgets to ask for a detail still passes. An LLM user with a goal and hidden details behaves like a real customer and exposes those gaps.

interview.question: What is pass^k and why report it?
interview.answer: The probability that all k independent runs of a scenario succeed. Users meet the agent many times; an agent right 71% of the time succeeds on all four tries only about 25% of the time.

mistakes.mistake: Letting the simulator reveal every detail at once
mistakes.fix: Instruct it to reveal hidden details only when asked
Check the end state in the backend
